item.title: dear steve, i recently bought the game railroader and i have been spending all my time playing it rather than doing my calculus work, how should i go about resolving this issue? also, how's the weather where you are? it's nice and overcast here
item.description:
11.1.26 4:59 pm
Q: dear steve, i recently bought the game railroader and i have been spending all my time playing it rather than doing my calculus work, how should i go about resolving this issue? also, how's the weather where you are? it's nice and overcast here
A: my name's not steve but anyway what you wanna do is, while you're playing the train game, begin to understand at least how your homework works. how many things there are to do, etc. then pick out the first thing you WOULD have to do, hypothetically, if you were doing the homework, and just begin to think about that while playing the train game. in times of need, you always wanna see if you can get curiosity to do the heavy lifting

item.description:
11.1.26 8:39 pm

A: i think one of the primary features of this particular song will have to be that you don't totally know what you're doing. sometimes when you try to hide that, things get awkward. but when you show that, it can be magical in a way that you may only realize later

A: the whole key to this is finding the fun. if you can't find the fun then the whole thing breaks down. i know you are trying to explain that there is currently no fun, and you are aware of this, and i agree this is a major problem. but i think the fun can be found, even within the current stage

item.title: i wanna make songs but i get too distracted planning them out and making album art and all these things. is this good? is this a sign i should do something else? how can i stop? should i? any advice? is blue overrated? thank you wise one
item.description:
11.1.26 11:53 pm
Q: i wanna make songs but i get too distracted planning them out and making album art and all these things. is this good? is this a sign i should do something else? how can i stop? should i? any advice? is blue overrated? thank you wise one
A: sometimes it can be a very nice anchor to deal with titles, presentation, and cover art. sometimes you need that to help mythologize the piece. but the issue i think you might be dealing with is a very active mind, active curiosity, and active doubts. the doubts are really the only problem with this and i'm not sure if there is a good remedy for that without accidentally remedying the other two

item.description:

item.title: is there a reason you can never really decide on a definitive favourite thing or is that just a running gag for this web site
item.description:
11.4.26 2:23 pm
Q: is there a reason you can never really decide on a definitive favourite thing or is that just a running gag for this web site
A: in many cases, such as artistic or creative things, if it didnt work well enough to make me feel in that moment like it's the best thing in the world, then it means it really fell short. art and creativity has that power, so if it's doing its job, one way or another it will have swept me away, wowed me, at least enough for it to be impossible to exactly measure how it compares to any previous time something did that. and also part of the nature of being swept away like this is that it feels different than anything else quite feels. so even if it were truly measurable, it would mostly never be the same thing twice. i consider this a normal part of being wowed. But if we're talking about less artistic things, things with less of a wow factor, i would very well have favorites. but i don't always say all of them because i tend to portion them out over time, to always hopefully save something interesting to tell you later

item.title: i fucked up sooooo bad. i came up with a really nice chord progression and got carried away and added some light percussion and bass and it sounds good. and now i have 5-6 ideas for a melody on top, none of which sound good or catchy. I know your strategy is famously to do the chords and the melody and the lyrics at the same time, and i normally do things this way too (or at least, within minutes of each other) but now its TOO LATE! Its been several days!!! Am i screwed!! Do i have to just throw this away now! i literally can't come up with anything to sing on top of it. It's like there was a window of time where I could have come up with something magic but now anything i do has absolutely no soul in it because im trying to fill a melody shaped gap. I'm so depressed about this its insane.
item.description:
11.8.26 12:42 am
Q: i fucked up sooooo bad. i came up with a really nice chord progression and got carried away and added some light percussion and bass and it sounds good. and now i have 5-6 ideas for a melody on top, none of which sound good or catchy. I know your strategy is famously to do the chords and the melody and the lyrics at the same time, and i normally do things this way too (or at least, within minutes of each other) but now its TOO LATE! Its been several days!!! Am i screwed!! Do i have to just throw this away now! i literally can't come up with anything to sing on top of it. It's like there was a window of time where I could have come up with something magic but now anything i do has absolutely no soul in it because im trying to fill a melody shaped gap. I'm so depressed about this its insane.
A: there's no need to panic. all you have to do is just admit that it happened. Even if your preferred way to write is to involve the melody and words altogether all the time, there are still totally different games to play. it's not what you normally do, but it's lucky that you get a chance to try it for this one. This particular song truly is based on a "cool chord progression". put it aside for now and just be glad that you have one of those "cool chord progression" songs, which as you say is not how you prefer to work, but at least now you have a chance to try it from time to time. i have a couple of things like that too, where a 'chord sequence' really is the main attraction. like you, i dont prefer to work that way, but it's nice that it occasionally does happen. if you put it aside for awhile, just being aware that you have something like this, eventually when you least expect it you will find the next step that excites you. the trick is not to be ashamed about the "hey man check out my cool chord progression" nature of this song. just accept that that's what kind of song this is, and take the chance to do what your version of that would be. maybe lean into it, make a melody that openly brags about how cool the chords are. admit what has happened, rather than hiding from it

item.title: Did you initially experience discomfort or frustration over an inability to precisely articulate musical concepts that originated within your musical subconscious? Have you ever attempted to collapse the liminal boundary between the idealism of a musical concept and its execution? If so, has this search brought you closer to expressing yourself musically? Lastly, what wisdom would you give to someone who is desperately trying to find their musical voice, but struggling to express it clearly. Is it a fault of methodology, or is it the fault of logic getting in the way of the somatic, intuitive aspects of musical expression? What are your views on this topic?
item.description:
11.10.26 3:29 am
Q: Did you initially experience discomfort or frustration over an inability to precisely articulate musical concepts that originated within your musical subconscious? Have you ever attempted to collapse the liminal boundary between the idealism of a musical concept and its execution? If so, has this search brought you closer to expressing yourself musically? Lastly, what wisdom would you give to someone who is desperately trying to find their musical voice, but struggling to express it clearly. Is it a fault of methodology, or is it the fault of logic getting in the way of the somatic, intuitive aspects of musical expression? What are your views on this topic?
A: i don't totally understand everything you said, but the connection between the music you imagine and the result that comes out will always get closer, just like the connection between words you want to say and the words you actually say. On the other hand, there will always be some slight bit of a difference, which can be embraced. in filmmaking, it is often said "a movie is made 3 times. when it's written, when it's put on camera, and when it's edited." Each time, you look at what you have, and in many ways it's different from what you thought it was gonna be. which can actually be somewhat awesome. But anyway, the more experience you have, the stronger all these things get, and the more accurately you'll be able to express yourself. while also developing a nice relationship with this small bit of unpredictability thrown in, and embrace that as well

item.title: I can't quite express what "hi" makes me feel. It's like a forgotten dream I myself have had but have never seen. It elicits a strange sense of deja vu. I am both baffled and impressed by your capturing of the subconscious feelings of a dream. So, good job. Why are the infinity busses so ominous??
item.description:
11.10.26 7:03 pm
Q: I can't quite express what "hi" makes me feel. It's like a forgotten dream I myself have had but have never seen. It elicits a strange sense of deja vu. I am both baffled and impressed by your capturing of the subconscious feelings of a dream. So, good job. Why are the infinity busses so ominous??
A: to write from the subconscious means we don't always know all the exact answers, but here are my top 10 best guesses of why the infinity bus might seem ominous, and i'm saying 10 hoping that i will be able to come up with 10 things which i havent yet: 1. it doesnt say anything 2. infinity is ominous 3. you have no idea what it does 4. it drives at least 500 miles per hour 5. it can brake from, and accelerate to, approximately 500 miles per hour, instantly 6. it seems to be tracking and targeting specific people, as well as listening to them 7. a character reacts to it with great alertness and urgency, as if it were not only some kind of mortal threat, but one that is well known 8. it apparently can multiply 9. it has an extremely subtle piece of musical underscoring which you may or may not realize you have heard before somewhere else 10. it leaves at the exact moment that the character says "goodbye". Not after, not before. if either one were reacting to the other, one would have occured before the other. but it occured at exactly the same time. which suggests a somewhat supernatural intertwinement with the character's consciousness 11. it adds crazy amounts of megabytes to the file size when i start duplicating them, because it was modeled for a closeup scene and therefore has an extremely high polygon count, which i ended up solving by just linking them. i could have also made a reduced polygon version for the distant overhead shot but that turned out not to be necessary

item.title: Dear mr wurtz, A couple things (Which I know fully well I may never see the answer to because it's kind of a couple-monthly routine to ask something here and then forget til the next time). I love music and it's all I can see myself wanting to do in the future - producing, writing, performing. Obviously not the most realistic set of goals one could have. But I have to do this university course as well which I'm not very good at and is kind of really boring. I've found recently that the time the course takes from me is often spent thinking about how much I want to work on my art. But then, after the time passes and the awakeness is drained from me, when I try to create it feels like my all isn't there (probably because i only have like 30% of my energy by that time). It makes me feel guilty. The craft I love and always want to work on feels like it's becoming an afterthought. I hate that. Recently I felt like I was making jumps in progress too, like really getting better at making my music. Sucks to live feeling like time is slipping away. I don't need or expect you to give me a solution to this problem. But as one artist to another I wonder if you've ever felt or experienced something similar. I appreciate your time reading and hope you have a good day, night or whatever lies inbetween (is that dusk? or dawn? both?).

item.title: when you sit down to write and every single idea immediately feels uncool or wrong to your own ears, do you force yourself to finish the 'bad' idea anyway, or is it better to simply move on to the next idea at times?
item.description:
11.10.26 10:32 pm
Q: when you sit down to write and every single idea immediately feels uncool or wrong to your own ears, do you force yourself to finish the 'bad' idea anyway, or is it better to simply move on to the next idea at times?
A: if i'm making new ideas for new things, then it's usually just very small bits to start. so if on one of them we're not feelin it, it's seriously no big deal. just like sabotage that one for now and it may be worth a laugh later OR it may actually seem good later (and/or both), you seriously never know. However, it's a totally different situation if you're working on a song. and you know that's the song you're working on. and you're trying to get the next part and you're just not getting it. in that case basically all you have to do is settle down and chill out until your mind wanders and you accidentally loosen up

item.title: if the past tense of shake is shook, why isn't the past tense of quake quook?
item.description:
11.11.26 2:55 am
Q: if the past tense of shake is shook, why isn't the past tense of quake quook?
A: it doesnt need to be. the only words that petition for special vowel modifications for the past tense are the ones that get a lot of use, and run the risk of being misunderstood. with 'quake' you'll be in trouble anyway even in the present tense if you dont firmly bring up 'earthquake'. However, if you find a scenario where 'quake' is being used a lot as a verb to describe some normal action, perhaps in a game or something, it's almost certain that you might find it necessary to start saying quook, in the past tense. it's only a matter of time before the next issue comes up, when you have to say "how much have you quooked so far" or "how much have you quaken so far"

item.title: what was the specific situation you were in when you came up with the infinity bus? it is a very intriguing / relatable concept to me and i suspect others and i wish to know more
item.description:
11.11.26 4:36 am
Q: what was the specific situation you were in when you came up with the infinity bus? it is a very intriguing / relatable concept to me and i suspect others and i wish to know more
A: it must have been immediately after i came up with the previous line. you can think of it this way, at that point in the video, everything that's been started so far has been wrapped up. went up stairs, needed a map, made a map. sang a song about where we are and we're going, and how we're feeling, we contemplate that as a mixtape, we leave the house with the other mixtape, deliver it to the record company. Everything's done. now we're back on the sidewalk casually riffing the previous refrain, then it's "ok, how bout i plan my day" right there at that moment we can do ANYTHING. i've firmly deluded myself into thinking i'm willing to go ANYWHERE, animate ANYTHING, i can make this character walk into any building, heck i can even make him go to the airport and get on a plane. So, as soon as i barely even realize just how much freedom i'm faced with, it is precisely at that moment that the infinity bus swoops in. So it is that exact situation on the sidewalk at that moment in the video that caused the infinity bus to come to mind

item.title: Hi Bill. Thank you for making the "hi" video, I really enjoyed it! Here is my working theory about it. Apologies if this reads like a badly written high school essay. I didn't plan to write down this much but I just needed to get my thoughts out of my head. Please feel free to ignore this if it's too much. I think the video is essentially about two parts of a single mind struggling to make sense of and say something about the world. The two parts are represented by not-shelby-person and Shelby, who have contrasting approaches to their understanding of and interactions with reality. Not-shelby-person and Shelby likely represent two parts of a single mind. When not-shelby-person begins to ask Shelby whether she has any mixtapes to be delivered, she instantly knows what is going to be asked and presents her mixtape. In the final song about the concert, the lyrics "i know, do you know?" are sung while both characters rapidly switch positions, representing a rapid conversation between two selves that are actually one person. The fact that not-shelby-person and Shelby are male and female also may allude to how both parts of the mind are needed to give birth two a new idea (represented by the 'concert'). Not-shelby-person has a very prescriptive approach in that he often tries to define and limit things. His hairstyle seems to resemble bricks, perhaps representing a desire to lay a foundation for his understanding of reality brick by brick. He attempts to know where he is, what things are, and how things are supposed to be. However, he fails at these attempts multiple times. He asks Shelby if her paper is double-sided, perhaps to know the full physical limit of her list. His attempt to define his location with the map ends up becoming self-referential ("a map of the map"). He says "trick or treat" at the door of the record company (isn't that what you're supposed to say at the door?) only to have to use the other door that says "use other door". He installs a second roof just to get it "taken care of". He also desires agency. His skateboard, which he controls with his legs, is representative of this. He doesn't get very far on it though, as seen when it gets stuck in a tree and when he keeps jumping back in place during his "good start" montage. Another image of stagnation is the clock, which doesn't seem to move past 10:14 throughout the video. He isn't oblivious to his failures, as in his "good start" montage he sings "I'm not sad, I don't feel bad", which could be him suppressing his true feelings or implying that he doesn't feel happy or good either. Due to not-shelby-person's obsession with (and failure at) defining and limiting the world into digestible chunks, he is in turn afraid of the "infinity bus", which represents the unlimited scope of the reality around him. The bus imagery evokes cyclical-ness (the wheels on the bus go round and round)and the loss of agency (you don't control the bus, as opposed to the skateboard). The bus appears three times: when he begins to plan his day, when he asks Shelby whether she wrote down the fact that she is writing everything down (self-referential), and after the final dialogue between not-shelby-person and Shelby (more on that later). All appearances occur when not-shelby-person starts to realize the unlimited and undefinable scope of everything. Shelby is almost a negation of not-shelby-person. She is very descriptive and observational, as seen in her writing down everything. Her hairstyle resembles planets, representing her interest in observing things in motion. She doesn't care about defining things with strict boundaries, as she ironically defines her definition-obsessed counterpart "not-shelby-person" (which by definition really could be anyone). But she also fails to capture every event, as she seemingly doesn't know where to start nor what to keep track of ("boats, roaring 20s, etc") and ends up becoming overwhelmed and scribbling everything. Of the 'concert', not-shelby-person says "Is that the concert we're supposed to write" (showing an active desire to do what he's supposed to), while Shelby replies "someone's gotta do it", showing her more passive nature. When working on the 'concert', not-shelby-person says he likes that "this doesn't go any further", pointing out the boundary of the paper. In response, Shelby says she likes "how it does go... as far as it does go". She then sings about wanting to know how far it goes, visualizing smaller and smaller waves until not-shelby-person stops her abruptly, perhaps a little scared by the infinite repetition. Shelby is willing to examine reality as it is without imposing any boundaries. This is why she doesn't seem to be afraid of the infinity buses. Her name "Shelby" might also be read as "shall be", as in, whatever shall be, shall be. Both not-shelby-person and Shelby want to understand and say something about the world, through either definitions and boundaries or through observation and record-keeping respectively. This reflects two types of interactions between the human mind and reality. Both of these interactions produce their own 'mixtapes' and their own projects (planning the day, writing down everything), which represent different approaches to making meaningful statements about reality. "Selling" is also a recurring theme, which could be read as the act of "selling" or convincing other people of a statement or observation of reality. The phone selling Shelby everything that she does ("got to go downstairs") might represent how phones, particularly through ads or social media, often try to convince others of a certain interpretation of their own reality. Both not-shelby-person and Shelby fail at "selling" their own interpretations of reality. Their mixtapes are received passively rather than enthusiastically by the record company. The concert, which becomes a collaborative project between the two, produces only adjectives ("great! amazing! wonderful!") and descriptions ("ends differently from how it starts" and "gets awards but still deserves more") with no grammatical subject, after which it quite literally falls flat. After witnessing this, the final dialogue ("I'd buy tickets to that!" "They don't sell tickets to that." "Sell tickets to what?" "Exactly.") confirms how "that" (the concert they had just witnessed) is undefinable and therefore cannot be "sold to" or be understood by others. Shelby's final statement "This must be why we're hiding in the basement" along with the shot of multiple infinity buses shows the futility of the mind's attempts at stating anything about reality without hiding from its boundless, undefinable scope.

item.title: love everything in the new video. does it feel great to 3D model so many details after the work is complete? it adds so much to my experience
item.description:
11.11.26 7:42 pm
Q: love everything in the new video. does it feel great to 3D model so many details after the work is complete? it adds so much to my experience
A: there is a spectrum of how much to model before camera, and how much to model after camera. this would be an example of an experiment to see what happens when you model just about everything before camera. The great advantage to this: when you finally show up with the camera, the world is your playground. you can find all kinds of groovy shots by putting the camera in all kinds of crazy places, and you find your shots based on all the great things that are there. The huge disadvantage is that it's extremely wasteful. you model so much stuff that will never be seen. It also has the tendency to make your camera look a little hyper, because you are desperately trying to show off all the cool stuff. The other end of the spectrum would be to model almost nothing (just basic blocks to indicate where things are), then do your camera, trying to imagine what could be there. then model things afterwards, playing only to the camera shots. this would obviously be way more efficient, but the disadvantage is that you don't get the magic of surprising yourself by what you see when you put the camera in different places. With this video (and many upcoming videos) i'm pretty sure i've figured out for sure that modeling everything before camera is not the best way to go. too wasteful. but it is a trade off

item.title: I'm currently finding myself in a musical slump, whenever I try to create anything right now I either create something that I am not happy with in the slightest or I end up going back to the same few things I've already used in previous songs. I've heard before that intentionally creating a "bad" song or songs can help with this, but I've found it just doesn't work for me. I still do want to create, though, despite the difficulty it's currently giving me. Do you have any tips for this problem? Any way to force myself to continue on with something I find bad, or alternatively, gain (and use) inspiration for something new?
item.description:
11.11.26 11:24 pm
Q: I'm currently finding myself in a musical slump, whenever I try to create anything right now I either create something that I am not happy with in the slightest or I end up going back to the same few things I've already used in previous songs. I've heard before that intentionally creating a "bad" song or songs can help with this, but I've found it just doesn't work for me. I still do want to create, though, despite the difficulty it's currently giving me. Do you have any tips for this problem? Any way to force myself to continue on with something I find bad, or alternatively, gain (and use) inspiration for something new?
A: it's almost as if you forgot why you want any of this. at least that's what it feels like in those moments when you remember, you'll say "i cant believe i forgot the whole point of this". it's shockingly easy to forget to have fun. and i can promise you, at the highest levels of professional creativity, this happens multiple times a day. you might as well plan for it. but it won't work until you have fun. which raises a perhaps silly but important question, and it's not "how do you have fun", it's the next layer deeper than that: "Do you want to have fun?" which may seem obvious, but then even if you claim 'yes', it raises the next question "does WHO want to have fun", which is a question that is ultimately answerable with music. Basically we're looking for ways to get you curious

item.title: What is a solution to procrastinating editing a video?
item.description:
11.12.26 11:24 pm
Q: What is a solution to procrastinating editing a video?
A: the trick is, you always forget how simple it actually could be. it's the most common problem for any creative project, and it can happen multiple times a day, forgetting this. There is a magic moment, somewhere in here, just when you're about to think all is lost, when suddenly you realize: "the instrument you have is the instrument you have." i want to say that again because it's such a serious point: "the instrument you have is the instrument you have." this is what you realize which suddenly launches you back into action, and then for about the next 32 seconds, everything goes so well that you are dazzled by what you can achieve by something so simple. then of course you immediately become intimidated by your newfound expectation of such dazzle, going forward. then you have to re-set again, "the instrument you have is the instrument you have." and it's always enough, because when would it ever not be

item.title: why do i suck so bad at soloing over the changes to the chick corea tune windows? like more than i normally suck with other standards.
item.description:
11.13.26 3:57 am
Q: why do i suck so bad at soloing over the changes to the chick corea tune windows? like more than i normally suck with other standards.
A: here's the big question: do you like the song? have you heard the song played by people who liked the song? (another way of saying this might be, have you heard the authentic original recording of this song) OR, equally viable, is your reading good enough that you have a clear enough idea of how the song sounds, and you like the song? really what it comes down to: if you dont like the song, that's going to make it hard to make anything happen with it. what you may eventually learn to do, similar to what professional actors do, is find some genuine way to like the song, even if you didn't at first. this is usually what is required in order to give a genuine performance. this particular artist is not afraid to reach for the stars, so you're going to see some unique twists you might not have heard other places. so it all comes down to whether you actually like some of those twists and turns

item.title: What's your project organization method when working on multiple projects?
item.description:
11.14.26 8:07 pm
Q: What's your project organization method when working on multiple projects?
A: i only tried that once, i had an assembly line system for a series of videos, where i do all of 1 task for all videos, then do all of the next task for all videos, in the same order. The great great advantage of this strategy is, it gives you a chance to get really good practice doing that task, and often there is a breakthrough that happens after a certain period of time where you figure out a better way to do it, and you wouldnt have had that breakthrough if you have to keep switching to the next task. The huge disadvantage of this, however, is you never get a chance to learn from your mistakes until it's too late

item.title: What's your approach to deciding song length? i often get caught between wanting a song to be long enough to fully explore it's ideas, and not wanting a song to overstay it's welcome/get boring. I'm curious how you approach this bc you have songs that can go up to 4 minutes long but also songs that are only a few seconds long. How do you feel about songs that are like, 10+ minutes of pure song?
item.description:
11.24.26 1:14 am
Q: What's your approach to deciding song length? i often get caught between wanting a song to be long enough to fully explore it's ideas, and not wanting a song to overstay it's welcome/get boring. I'm curious how you approach this bc you have songs that can go up to 4 minutes long but also songs that are only a few seconds long. How do you feel about songs that are like, 10+ minutes of pure song?
A: i've tried a lot of different things, for a lot of different reasons. but basically there is no separate decision of how long a song should be. it's just part of writing the song. in the course of trying to imagine what ought to happen next, at any moment, among the possibilities for what could happen next is, it could end. after many years songwriting and listening to a lot of songs, i can attest to a sweet spot of somewhere between 2:30 and 3:30. but it's great to sometimes do even shorter. i've found, and i always say this, when it gets any longer than that, it starts to really need some video and maybe some scenes and other non-song material to move the story along
